notes:
I could only read some of the sources you allowed, mostly through search-result extracts. Enduring Word, the Bible Hub and StudyLight commentary pages (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch, Barnes, Calvin, Clarke, Henry), bible.org (Utley) and one NET Bible note came through. Nothing turned up from the Orthodox or Catholic sites you listed (oca.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com), from Pentecostal sites other than Enduring Word, or from prosperity or word-of-faith teaching, so those are left out. Verses with nothing reliable are also left out.

## vv. 23–24: Joseph's birth

**v. 23:** Barnes says God "remembered" Rachel at the best time for her, after teaching her dependence and patience. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/genesis/30-24.html 

**v. 24 (the name):** Most commentators see a play on two Hebrew words: *asaph* ("taken away," looking back to v. 23) and *yasaph* ("add"). Barnes says double meanings are common in Bible names. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-24.html 

**v. 24 (was Rachel's wish good or bad?):** Commentators disagree here.
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** He reads it as "strong faith" that she would have another son. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-24.html 
- **Matthew Henry:** He allows two readings: greedy desire for more, or faith that takes this mercy as a pledge of more to come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/genesis/30.htm 
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** He takes the less kind view: Rachel felt vindicated but wanted more children to keep competing with Leah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/ 
- **Ellicott:** He sees no trace of triumph over Leah. He thinks Rachel had the covenant promises in mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-24.html 

**v. 24 (fulfilment):** Clarke (Wesleyan/Methodist) calls the name a prophecy, fulfilled in Benjamin's birth (Genesis 35:18). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-24.html  Ellicott notes that God did give her another son, but it cost her her life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-24.html 

**v. 24 ("God" in v. 23, "LORD" in v. 24):**
- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):** They explain the change without needing two sources. Rachel first looks back and sees the son as God's gift. Then her envy fades and she prays to the covenant LORD for another son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-24.htm 
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It agrees, seeing a higher spiritual life in Rachel, now free of human devices like the mandrakes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-24.html 
- **Modern scholarship (Cambridge Bible):** It explains the two meanings as coming from two source documents, called E and J. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-24.htm 

**v. 24 (Catholic view):** Haydock (Catholic, 1811) says Rachel looks both back and forward. She thanks God and asks for another son, a request that led to her death: "so little do we know what we ask for!" https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-24.html 

## vv. 25–34: Jacob and Laban strike a deal

**v. 25:** Barnes says Jacob could not ask to leave until his 14 years were up. So Joseph was born at the earliest in Jacob's fifteenth year with Laban. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/genesis/30-24.html  Guzik notes that after 14 years Jacob still called the Promised Land "my country." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/

**v. 26:** Barnes thinks Jacob expected Laban to give him at least the means to make the journey home. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-27.html 

**v. 27 ("divination"):** Commentators split on this word.
- **Laban practised the occult:** Guzik says it literally means "learned by divination" and that Laban probably practised occult divination. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/  Gill reports Jewish readers who saw Laban as a diviner using his household idols (teraphim). He adds a doubt that the devil would give such a strong witness to the LORD and to Jacob. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-27.htm 
- **It just means he noticed:** Barnes renders it "I have been an attentive observer." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-27.html  Clarke reads it as studying Jacob's conduct closely. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-27.html  Ellicott thinks the word had lost its special meaning, so Laban only means "I fancy." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-27.htm 
- **Laban's flattery:** Ellicott calls the answer courtly and complimentary but inconclusive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-27.htm  The Cambridge Bible points out that Laban's sentence is left unfinished in Hebrew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-27.htm 
- **Application:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls this proof that good people bring blessing to the places they live. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-27.htm  The Bible Hub study notes link it to the promise "I will bless those who bless you" (Genesis 12:3). https://biblehub.com/genesis/30-27.htm 

**v. 28:** Barnes says Laban leaves Jacob to set the wage and binds himself to pay it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-27.html 

**vv. 29–30:** Barnes explains two phrases: "brake forth" means increased, and "at my foot" means under Jacob's care. Jacob is pointing out what his work has been worth, perhaps feeling Laban owes him fairly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-36.htm 

**v. 31:** Barnes says "you shall not give me anything" shows Jacob started with no animals from Laban. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-36.htm  Matthew Henry says Jacob left his case to God rather than agreeing a fixed wage with a very selfish Laban. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-36.htm 

**v. 32:**
- **Rare colours:** Barnes explains that in the East sheep are usually white and goats dark, so spotted ones were rare. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-35.html 
- **Future animals only:** He says Jacob's wage was the spotted young born later, not the ones removed now, because Jacob chose to depend wholly on God for his pay. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-35.html 
- **A deal against Jacob:** Guzik notes that removing the spotted animals first made the odds worse for Jacob. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/ 

**v. 33:** Barnes says the colour would show at once whose each animal was. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-35.html  Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) reads "my honesty will testify" as Jacob leaving it to God to prove him in the right. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-35.html 

**v. 34:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the offer seemed so much in Laban's favour that he agreed at once. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-35.htm 

## vv. 35–36: Laban moves the spotted animals away

**v. 35 (what Laban did):** Keil & Delitzsch say Laban made the selection himself, "probably to make more sure." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-35.htm  The Cambridge Bible says Jacob would start with nothing in his favour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-35.htm 

**v. 35 (whose sons?):** Gill says they were Laban's sons, because Reuben was not yet seven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-35.htm  Ellicott disagrees. He puts Reuben at 26 and argues Jacob's flocks would have fared badly in the hands of Laban's sons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-35.htm  The Pulpit Commentary lists scholars on both sides. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-35.htm 

**v. 36:** Calvin (Reformed) says the distance was meant to stop the flocks mixing and producing spotted young. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-35.html  The NET Bible quotes the scholar E. A. Speiser: Laban, delighted with the terms, at once broke the spirit of the deal. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Gen&chapter=30  Benson notes that the Samaritan text puts the angel's dream (Genesis 31) at this point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-35.htm 

## vv. 37–43: The peeled branches

**The main debate:** Did the branches actually work, and was Jacob in the right? Commentators split on this, but the lines don't follow denominations.
- **God told Jacob to do it:** Poole and the Geneva Bible say Jacob acted on God's command, citing Genesis 31. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-37.htm  Matthew Henry agrees: it was done at God's prompting, as a sign of his power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-36.htm 
- **Shrewd, but God was behind it:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown admits it is hard to clear Jacob of some pretence. Still, it sees "something miraculous" in Genesis 31. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-36.htm 
- **Calvin:** He grants the account may at first seem absurd, but says the context shows Jacob was not at fault. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-37.html 
- **The branches did nothing:** Coffman says it was either superstition or a test of faith commanded by God. He firmly denies the branches produced the spotted young. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-37.html  Utley says the cause was God's supernatural presence, not Jacob's tricks. He calls this "Jacob, the trickster" trying to help God keep his promises. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-30 
- **Jacob did his best and God blessed it:** Guzik's view. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-30/ 
- **It was natural cause and effect:** Barnes says experience had taught Jacob that what the mothers saw at breeding affected the colour of their young. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-37.htm  Ellicott calls the result "physically certain." https://biblehub.com/genesis/30-37.htm 

**v. 37:** Gill says "fresh" means newly cut and moist, and that the peeled bands made the branches look many-coloured. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-37.html  The Pulpit Commentary notes that ancient translators disagreed over which trees are meant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-37.htm 

**vv. 38–39:** Keil & Delitzsch say the mottled branches were placed in the troughs so that mating at drinking time would happen near them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-37.htm  The Bible Hub notes deny it was magic. They see it as an ordinary step God used to show his control (Genesis 31:12). https://biblehub.com/genesis/30-37.htm 

**v. 40:** Barnes says Jacob turned the flock to face the rare-coloured young, to have the same effect as the branches. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-37.htm  Keil & Delitzsch say Jacob kept his own spotted flock apart so Laban's animals would always have it in view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-37.htm 

**vv. 41–42:** Barnes calls using the branches only with the strong animals Jacob's "second device." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-37.htm  Coffman says this selective breeding is often overlooked. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/30-37.html 

**v. 43 (and the link to Genesis 31):** Guzik says the dream in Genesis 31:10–13 shows Jacob had more than clever farming methods: he had God's blessing. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/genesis/genesis-31.cfm  Utley, on Genesis 31, credits God's grace rather than Jacob's methods. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-31  Matthew Henry argues Laban had no grounds to complain: Jacob got only what was agreed, and Laban gained greatly from his work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/30-35.htm
